reason: Phyllaries are often cobwebby (arachnose, arachnoid), and the examples are correct.
A velvety sepal surface is normal and the examples are correct.
Lateral veins can fork or branch, and the examples show this.
A spur or short shoot can be swollen. The French 'enflé' examples fit too.
'Entire' describes the margin, and the examples say 'margin entire'. The bearer should be leaf margin, so a rule is needed to move margin words to the margin part.
A papery leaf sheath is normal, as in grasses.
The examples are about the apex or base of the pinna, which are separate parts. The generic attribute 'sharpness' also carries no value.

Most examples compare the bracteole with another organ ('shorter than calyx'). That belongs to a comparison pattern, not a plain quality. A rule would need to separate absolute 'short' from relative 'shorter than X'.
Pappus colour (straw, white, burnt-orange) is a standard character.
The examples are 'rays' of umbels with pedicels, not Asteraceae ray flowers. This is a wrong part reading, so a rule is needed to tell umbel rays from ray florets.
Filaments can be entire, or toothed or appendaged, so the contrast is meaningful.
Frond texture (herbaceous, coriaceous) is normal in ferns.
Bract persistence (persistent or deciduous) is a standard character.
Inflorescence branches can be ascending.
Sunken (impressed) secondary veins are a common leaf character.

The botanical term is 'discolorous' (upper and lower sides differ in colour), but PATO 'discolored' may mean a changed colour. A rule would need to confirm the PATO definition and use a two-sided colour pattern.
A subulate (awl-shaped) blade is normal.
'Equal' and 'unequal' compare the lobes with each other, not with a size value. A rule would need to treat equality among sister parts as its own pattern.
A matted growth form belongs to the whole plant.
The examples describe hairs, not the blade ('hairs slender'). This is a wrong part reading. Hairs should be the bearer.
Pappus bristles can be scabrid or barbellate, and these are texture values.
The count of lobes (or segments) of a stipule is a counted-part pattern.
'Suckering' means root-borne shoots are present, and the examples are correct.
A smooth leaf margin is normal.
Lobes can be obovate.
Veins can be conspicuous or evident.
Perianth lobes can be oblong.
Capsules can be furrowed, often when dry.
The number of disc glands is a counted-part pattern.
Leaf sheaths can be bristly (setose).
Roots can be conical or carrot-shaped.
Keeled (carinate) bracteoles are a normal character. The PATO term is close enough to 'carinate'.
The length-to-width ratio of a blade is a standard character.
The examples mostly say 'apex obtuse' or 'base rounded', so the bearer is the apex or base, not the pinna. A rule would need to move apex and base words to those parts.
'Prolonged beyond the collar' describes an extension relative to another structure, not a length. A rule would need to give prolongation its own pattern.
Stems can be floccose.
The outline of a capsule (ovate, oblong) is a normal shape character.
The examples are cell length-to-width ratios and row counts of leaf cells, not a count of plant cells. This is a wrong reading.
These 'rays' are umbel or inflorescence rays, not ray flowers. This is the same wrong part reading as ray flower and spreading.
A stalk (stipe) can be present or absent. Several examples are lengths, which another quality should handle.
A blade can be undivided.
Branches can be pendent.
The examples are about the apex or the margin ('upper margins rounded'), not the whole pinnule. A rule would need to move apex and margin words to those parts.
A leaf tip can be rough (scabrid), and the examples are correct. They all come from one flora.
Roots can be fascicled, such as storage roots in clusters.
Moss alar cells have a width, and the examples are measurements.
Blades can be plicate (pleated).
Petals or petal laminas can be rhombic.
Sepals can be ascending.
Blades can be spotted or maculate.
'Capillary' means hair-thin, not fibrillate (made of fibrils). The PATO term means something else, so a thin-or-filiform term should be used.
A legume can be stipitate or sessile, which is a stalked-or-not contrast.
'Dentate' and 'denticulate' describe the margin, so the bearer should be leaf margin. This is the same margin-word rule as lamina and entire.
Calyx lobes can be glabrous.
Stipule persistence (persistent or caducous) is a standard character, and the French examples are correct.
Teeth can be erect, and the examples are correct.
A corolla lip can have a ciliate margin, and the examples are correct.
Nodes can be glabrous, as in grass culm nodes.
The examples are rhizome scales (peltate or pseudopeltate), not trichomes on the shoot axis. This is a wrong part reading. Scales should be the bearer.
'Structure' is a generic attribute. Dehiscent or indehiscent is a dehiscence quality and should use a dehiscence term.
